documents: Bogolub, K. R., & Jones, C. H. (2022). Quantifying the cryptic topography of the High Plains. Tectonics, 41, e2022TC007370 (published PDF, 15 pages; Supporting Information not supplied)

entry.evidence: The cause and timing of this epeirogeny has yet to be satisfactorily explained.

steps.action: The authors pose the unsolved question of the cause and timing of the High Plains epeirogeny: the region is undeformed yet elevated more than 2 km.
steps.quote: The cause and timing of this epeirogeny has yet to be satisfactorily explained.

steps.action: The authors list published rival uplift mechanisms: lithospheric thinning or removal, basal traction, mantle or crustal hydration, melt extraction, and past or present dynamic topography.
steps.quote: Thinning of mantle lithosphere either by thermal erosion of lithosphere

steps.action: The authors design a discriminating approach: remove the observable effects so that the spatial extent of the remaining topography can be set against the rivals' differing footprints.
steps.quote: one means of distinguishing among these might be to determine the geographic extent and/or timing of the creation of topography

steps.action: The authors refine the question: how much High Plains topography remains after sedimentation and flexure are removed? This directly tests the Mitrovica et al. (1989) sedimentation hypothesis.
steps.quote: determining how much topography in the High Plains remains after observable processes are considered

steps.action: The authors take the top of the Cretaceous Dakota Formation, deposited near sea level, as a paleo-horizontal reference surface known from traces.
steps.quote: Therefore the top of this formation can be used a reference surface

steps.action: The authors compile Dakota depths from COGCC and KGS well logs, keeping 11,000 of 20,000 logs, and map and interpolate the Dakota along three east-west profiles to get load thickness.
steps.quote: We used 11,000 of the 20,000 well logs examined, rejecting duplicates and outliers

steps.action: The authors digitize density logs and fit an exponential density-depth function separately to mountain and plains wells, keeping the fit and fit ±RMSD as three density models.
steps.quote: the data from each subset of wells, the mountain and plains wells, were fit to the function

steps.action: The authors estimate two flexural rigidities by fitting an analytic foredeep flexure solution to the Fox Hills Formation shape of the Denver Basin. They treat these as lower bounds because the profiles are 1D.
steps.quote: We obtained two estimates for flexural rigidity by modeling the Denver Basin as a foredeep basin.

steps.action: The authors adopt a third, higher flexural rigidity from the gravity and topography analysis of Lowry and Pérez-Gussinyé (2011).
steps.quote: We used another set of flexural rigidities based on the work by Lowry and Pérez-Gussinyé (2011)

steps.action: The authors check the forebulge position implied by the cited rigidity against the known eastward extent of Denver Basin strata and treat that rigidity as an upper bound.
steps.quote: This appears to be unrealistically far given the absence of Denver Basin strata more than ∼300 km east

steps.action: The authors run a synthetic trapezoidal-load test of the load-thickness method. It shows that the simple method underestimates the true load (about 1.5 times the area).
steps.quote: Figure 6 illustrates a case where a simple trapezoidal load is set upon a horizontal surface

steps.action: The authors define four Rocky Mountain load geometries: a 1.2× scaled load, a horizontal base, and two lower end-member bases.
steps.quote: four different estimates of the load geometry were used

steps.action: The authors solve the variable-rigidity plate flexure equation by finite differences for all 36 parameter combinations and subtract each deflection from the present Dakota to obtain cryptic topography. It is higher to the west and south.
steps.quote: we calculated 36 different deflections along each of our profiles

steps.action: The authors run one-at-a-time sensitivity tests on density (118–165 m), flexural rigidity (81–198 m) and load geometry (379–431 m, confined to the western 60–80 km).
steps.quote: we plotted the range of cryptic topography with two of the parameters held constant and varying the third parameter

steps.action: The authors compare the residual 1,000–1,500 m (750–1,250 m after Cretaceous sea level) with the Mitrovica et al. prediction that sedimentation and flexure account for the modern topography.
steps.quote: our cryptic topography profiles indicate between 1,000–1,500 m of topography in the High Plains cannot be explained

steps.action: The authors reject the sedimentation-in-a-dynamic-trough mechanism as the sole explanation; it accounts for at most half of the elevation.
steps.quote: That process explains no more than half of the present elevations of the High Plains at these latitudes.

steps.action: The authors set their estimate against published estimates: it is consistent with Levandowski et al. (2018), about twice Spencer (1996), and similar to Humphreys et al. (2015) for the sediment contribution.
steps.quote: notably consistent with the conclusion of Levandowski et al. (2018)

steps.action: The authors check the north-to-south increase against a topographic profile at 38°N, where the Dakota is at or near the surface.
steps.quote: We think that higher amount of cryptic topography in the south is present in a topographic profile at 38°N

steps.action: The authors derive qualitative spatial uplift patterns for four rival classes: magmatic depletion, Rio Grande Rift upwelling, Liu & Gurnis dynamic topography, and narrow flat-slab hydration (Figure 11).
steps.quote: Figure 11 compares several qualitative predictions of spatial surface uplift patterns from these different hypotheses

steps.action: The authors compare the cryptic topography contours with each predicted pattern. The match is best for magmatism or rift upwelling, poorer for dynamic topography and the narrow slab; the eastern extent needs some slab or dynamic component.
steps.quote: appears to be most consistent with magmatism focused on the San Juan Volcanic Field or rift upwelling

steps.action: The authors compare the eastward slope of the cryptic surface with published late Cenozoic tilting and dynamic topography estimates to discuss timing.
steps.quote: similar to the 1 m/km tilt attributed to regional tilting in the last 5 Ma predicted by Riihimaki et al. (2007)

steps.action: The authors retain the estimate of a broad ENE-dipping cryptic surface, 1.5 km at 39°N and about 1 km at 40°N on the western edge, unexplained by sedimentation and thrust loading.
steps.quote: This amount of unexplained topography shows that the present-day elevation of the High Plains cannot be explained by sedimentation and thrust loading alone

tree.answer: Elevated (>2 km), undeformed High Plains whose uplift since the Cretaceous is unexplained
No; cryptic topography is latent and is inferred by removing flexural effects from well-log data
Quantify the topography unexplained by sedimentation and thrust loading, and its spatial pattern
Yes; many published uplift mechanisms, with Mitrovica et al. (1989) addressed directly
Partly; rivals differ in qualitative spatial footprints (Figure 11) and in the share explained by sedimentation
Found; the Dakota Formation serves as a past near-sea-level horizon
Yes; the 1–1.5 km residual persists across 36 parameter combinations and one-at-a-time sensitivity tests
The sedimentation hypothesis explains at most half; the pattern is most consistent with magmatism or rift upwelling
Not shown; no review file supplied

end.claim: Between about 1 and 1.5 km of topography at the western edge of the High Plains (39–40°N) is cryptic: unexplained by post-Dakota sedimentation, thrust loading and flexure. It forms a broad planar surface dipping ENE, with uncertainty ranges set by sensitivity analysis.

decisive_move.sentence: The finite-difference flexure calculation over 36 combinations of density, rigidity and load geometry, subtracted from the well-log Dakota surface, produces the cryptic topography estimate; without it no residual could be stated.

gates.evidence: Action: the design was framed to address the Mitrovica et al. (1989) hypothesis (p. 2), but the data are archival well logs not acquired for this test. Claim: the residual could have been near zero had sedimentation and flexure explained the topography; the authors found 1–1.5 km and concluded that process explains no more than half (p. 12). Registration: nothing is stated as fixed before the data. The load factor of 1.2 was chosen after seeing that 1.5 gives unrealistically large deflections (p. 7).

imports.item: finite difference solution of the variable-rigidity plate flexure equation (Flex2D Matlab code, Chapman 2015)

imports.field: petroleum industry / state oil and gas regulation
imports.item: COGCC and Kansas Geological Survey well logs (formation tops and density logs)

novelty_claims.quote: We term this amount of unexplained topography cryptic topography.

limits: The Supporting Information (Text S1–S3, Table S1, Figure S1) was not supplied. The rigidity estimates and the density-fit parameters described there could not be checked. Outlier-rejection criteria for the 9,000 discarded well logs are not stated. No review file was supplied; the acknowledgments name reviewers A. Lowry and E. Humphreys, both authors of cited rival work, so referee influence on the text cannot be traced (inference). Time-dependent and dynamic effects are assumed second-order and are not tested. Sub-claims and their statuses: (a) the Mitrovica et al. sedimentation mechanism explains no more than half of the elevation, an exclusion as sole cause, roughly confirmed against the residual; (b) the spatial pattern is most consistent with magmatism or rift upwelling, best_explanation, from qualitative and loosely drawn rival patterns (the authors call the test challenging given limited extent); (c) the north-to-south increase is supported only by an informal 38°N topographic profile, a tentative regularity. Composition is none_fits. The walk is an estimation-by-subtraction from a past reference horizon with sensitivity analysis, followed by a qualitative comparison against rivals. It is not a crucial test (strong_inference), nor a series of independent traces standing in for varied auxiliaries (trace_series); the variation is of parameters, not of traces.

disagreements.target: Mitrovica et al. (1989) hypothesis that post-Cretaceous sedimentation in a dynamic trough plus flexural response accounts for modern High Plains topography
disagreements.support: After removing the sedimentary and thrust-load flexural contribution, 750–1,250 m (1,000–1,500 m before sea-level correction) remains, so the mechanism explains at most half.
disagreements.quote: That process explains no more than half of the present elevations of the High Plains at these latitudes.

disagreements.target: Spencer (1996) estimate of 1 km of elevation from sedimentation in Colorado's High Plains
disagreements.support: Their well-log-based thickness and density with flexure give about half Spencer's sedimentary contribution; they note Spencer assumed a full 3 km of sediment and ignored thrust loading.
disagreements.quote: It is higher by about a factor of two than inferred by Spencer (1996), who assumed a full 3 km of sediment

disagreements.target: Lowry and Pérez-Gussinyé (2011) flexural rigidities as applied to the Denver Basin
disagreements.support: The implied zero-deflection point lies [...] km east of the Colorado-Kansas border, beyond the extent of Denver Basin strata, so the authors treat these rigidities as upper bounds.
disagreements.quote: This appears to be unrealistically far given the absence of Denver Basin strata more than ∼300 km east

disagreements.target: Dynamic topography uplift model of Liu and Gurnis (2010)
disagreements.support: Cryptic topography contours decrease northward more rapidly than the predicted dynamic topography uplift pattern.
disagreements.quote: we see a more rapid decrease in cryptic topography northward than the predicted uplift patterns

disagreements.target: Narrow flat-slab hydration uplift pattern as envisioned by Saleeby (2003)
disagreements.support: The cryptic topography contours match the narrow-slab pattern poorly; a different slab incidence angle might fit better.
disagreements.quote: [...] contour lines do not match up particularly well with the narrow slab uplift pattern
